list.listitem: Infantile hemangiomas (IHs) are common benign vascular tumors of the skin. History and physical examination are sufficient to diagnose 95% of IHs. C
It is important to differentiate IHs from other vascular anomalies (see ). C

Most IHs are medically insignificant and asymptomatic, resolve spontaneously, and do not require treatment. Treatment is recommended when IHs pose life-threatening complications, are associated with underlying anomalies, or cause functional impairment, disfigurement, or ulceration. C
When treatment is indicated, use oral propranolol 2-3 mg/kg/day as first-line therapy for IHs in infants and children. B
Topical timolol maleate appears as effective as oral propranolol and is recommended for small, thin, superficial IHs. B

Second-line therapy includes surgical interventions and laser therapy to treat residual skin changes after involution and to manage certain types of IHs. Third-line therapies include becaplermin gel for ulcerated lesions, inteferon alpha, cytotoxins, cyclophosphamide, and angiogenesis inhibitors. C
IHs are often a cause of distress for parents and may have a negative psychological impact on school-aged children. Education is an important part of therapy. C
IHs can be part of serious and sometimes life-threatening syndromes, such as PHACES syndrome, SACRAL syndrome, PELVIS syndrome, and disseminated neonatal hemangiomatosis. C

background.definition: IHs are common benign vascular tumors of the skin characterized by rapid growth during the first few months of life followed by slow involution lasting a few years which concludes at a median age of 3 years.

list.listitem: Female to male ratio is 5:1, but is 9:1 in PHACES syndrome.
Approximately one-third of hemangiomas are present at birth and the remainder appear in the first several weeks of life.
Incidence is 21% in infants born to mothers who had prenatal chorionic villus sampling.
Twenty-two percent to 30% of preterm infants with birthweight less than 1 kg have IHs.
IHs are more common in white infants (10%-12%) than in those of African-American, Hispanic, or Asian descent.
IHs are the most common tumors in children with a prevalence between 4% and 5%.
The etiology of IHs is unclear but involves endothelial cell proliferation.
Risk factors include chorionic villus sampling, preterm birth, and white race.
They are associated with a number of congenital syndromes.

IHs are benign lesions with increased numbers of blood vessels. They show proliferating, plump endothelial cells with high mitotic rates and stromal components, such as fibroblasts, mast cells, stem cells and pericytes.

During the third trimester of fetal development, immature endothelial cells coexist with immature pericytes, which maintain their proliferative capacity for a limited period during postnatal life. Angiogenic peptides induce proliferation of these immature cells, resulting in the development of IHs.

As the endothelial cells differentiate, an influx of mast cells, various myeloid cells, and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) occurs. TIMPs terminate the endothelial cell proliferation and passively induce involution by senescence of endothelial cells.

IHs are usually single (80%), measuring a few mm to 5 cm in size, but may be larger or multiple. They are characterized by rapid growth during the first few months of life followed by slow involution lasting a few years which concludes at a median age of 3 years. C
Classify IHs based on type (ie, focal, segmental, or indeterminate), since the type portends risk (eg, segmental IHs are associated with complications). C
Differentiate IHs from other vascular anomalies because prognosis and treatment vary (see ). C
Ultrasound and MRI may be useful for the evaluation of deep, segmental, and syndromic IHs. C

IHs are usually single (80%), measuring a few mm to 5 cm in size. Less frequently they are larger (>20 cm in diameter) or multiple. Every part of the body may be affected, even though 60% of IHs occur on the head and neck, 25% on the trunk, and 15% on the extremities.

Classify IHs based on type (ie, focal, segmental, or indeterminate), since the type portends risk. Focal IHs, the commonest type, are raised, localized, and tumor-like. Segmental IHs, which are associated with complications, are big, broad, appear as plaques, follow a linear or segmental geographic pattern, and affect at least one embroylogic segment. Segmental IHs have a markedly higher risk of being life- or function-threatening, and/or may be markers for underlying malformations or developmental anomalies of the heart, blood vessels, or nervous system. Indeterminate IHs have features of both focal and segmental IHs.

The appearance of IHs may be subtle at birth; some do not become apparent for several days to months. Their appearance is affected by the depth of their location within the skin (ie, superficial, deep, or mixed). Superficial IHs appear as bright red or crimson raised nodules. Deep IHs involve the deeper dermis or subcutaneous tissue and may appear less demarcated and give an appearance of normal skin overlying soft masses with a bluish tone. Mixed IHs combine the features of superficial and deep IHs.

A 2016 Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) comparative effectiveness review on the diagnosis and management of IHs recommends having a high index of suspicion for extracutaneous IHs among patients with multiple skin lesions or facial involvement with a beard distribution. They recommend early referral for further evaluation and possible treatment for these children.
See "Natural history" for typical progression of IHs and association with congenital syndromes.

Doppler ultrasonography is a good first choice to help differentiate IHs from malformations or other tumors. It has the advantage of being accessible, minimally invasive, and inexpensive. Using this modality, proliferative IHs display high vessel density, high Doppler shift, low resistance, and little or no evidence of arteriovenous shunting. Unfortunately, the value of this examination can depend on the familiarity of the radiologist with these tumors, and the extent of the tumors is not well defined. Ultrasonography has a sensitivity of 95% for hepatic IHs.

MRI is the imaging modality of choice to delineate the location and extent of both cutaneous and extracutaneous hemangiomas. MRI also helps in differentiating arteriovenous malformations from proliferating IHs. MRI shows IHs as well-circumscribed, lobulated masses with feeding and draining vessels at the center and periphery. Flow voids are seen on spin-echo images, and enhancement with gadolinium is diffuse. MRI has a 100% sensitivity for intraspinal IHs, wheres ultrasound is only 20% sensitive.

Other imaging options include computed tomography, angiography, infrared thermography, three-dimensional stereophotogrammetry, and multichannel color imaging. Three-dimensional stereophotogrammetry may be a promising, fast, accurate, noninvasive way to determine and compare volumetric changes in IHs, and to evaluate therapeutic response.
Plain radiography may be useful for evaluating IHs that impinge on the airway.
Consider thyroid function testing in case of very large cutaneous or hepatic IHs.

A skin biopsy can be helpful in distinguishing unusual or atypical IHs from other vascular lesions. An immunophenotypic marker such as GLUT1 stains 100% of IHs. Other vascular lesions, including vascular malformations and kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas, fail to demonstrate expression of these markers.
History and physical examination are sufficient to diagnose 95% of IHs.
It is important to differentiate benign, common IHs from other vascular anomalies including malformations and tumors (), because their pathophysiology, treatment, and prognosis are different.

It is essential for primary care physicians to recognize typical and high-risk features of IHs, monitor patients monthly during early infancy for IH growth and complications, and refer high-risk patients to IH specialists

Most IHs are in anatomically neutral locations and involute without intervention. Treatment is recommended when IHs pose life-threatening complications, are associated with underlying anomalies, or cause functional impairment, disfigurement, or ulceration. C
When treatment is indicated, use oral propranolol 2-3 mg/kg/day as first-line therapy for IHs in infants and children. B
Topical timolol maleate appears as effective as oral propranolol and is recommended for small, thin, superficial IHs. B

Second-line therapy includes surgical interventions and laser therapy to treat residual skin changes after involution and to manage certain types of IHs. Third-line therapies include becaplermin gel for ulcerated lesions, inteferon alpha, cytotoxins, cyclophosphamide, and angiogenesis inhibitors. C
If treatment is indicated, first-line therapy involves systemic or topical beta-blockers.

A Cochrane review evaluating interventions for IHs of the skin found oral propranol and topical timolol to be more effective than placebo in causing clearance or resolution of lesions, without increasing harms. No difference in efficacy was found between oral propranolol and topical timolol, but safety comparisons yielded uncertain findings. Overall evidence was limited due to small sample sizes and risk of bias among included studies.

The 2016 AHRQ review found a high mean clearance rates for oral propranolol (95%, 95% BCI: 88%-99%) and moderate evidence of harm (eg, hypotension, bradycardia, hypoglycemia, sleep disturbances, and cold extremities). Topical timolol for small, superficial IHs is supported by low certainty evidence, but based on their meta-analysis it had the second highest mean estimate of expected clearance at 62%.

The 2019 American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) clinical practice guideline for the management of IHs recommends using oral propranolol at a dose of 2-3 mg/kg/day divided into 2 daily doses maintained for at least 6 months. In addition, it approves timolol maleate 0.5% gel-forming ophthalmic solution as a topical treatment of small, thin, and superficial IHs.

Combined oral and topical beta-blockers for early proliferative superficial periocular infantile capillary haemangioma were studied in a small RCT enrolling 25 patients. The topical and systemic group were treated with oral propanolol (1 mg/kg per day increased to 2 mg/kg in 2 weeks) and timolol maleate 0.5% gel. The systemic only group received the same dose of oral propanolol and simple eye ointment. The main outcomes were size change, proliferative activity and treatment side effects. The hemangioma activity score was significantly improved in both groups but significantly better in topical and systemic treatment group (p<0.05). There were no recorded serious local or systemic complications in either group.
A small RCT (N = 71) showed that oral nadolol was noninferior to oral propranolol for the treatment of IH.

The combined use of topical brimonidine 0.2%-timolol 0.5% may have a synergistic effect by targeting IHs via two mechanisms (alpha-agonism and beta-inhibition). However, the risk of unintended symptoms should always be considered when prescibing this off-label treatment.
Imiquimod 5% cream may accelerate the regression of proliferating IHs.

Prior to the universal use of beta-blockers for the primary management of IHs, systemic and intralesional corticosteroids were widely used. The 2016 AHRQ report found oral steroids to have moderate efficacy, with a 43% expected clearance rate compared to placebo or observation which was at 6%. However, it carried moderate evidence of harm (eg, hypertension, Cushingoid facies, infection, mood changes, growth retardation). Intralesional corticosteroid injection of bulky, localized IHs is supported by low certainty evidence, with a 58% expected clearance rate, and moderate evidence of harm (eg, skin atrophy).

Systemic and intralesional corticosteroids should only be considered among children who have failed to respond to or have absolute contraindications to beta-blockers. Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide, 10 to 40 mg/mL, at doses of 3 to 5 mg/kg per treatment session, may be injected for small lesions on the lip, nasal tip, cheek, or ear, but must be utilized with caution in periorbital IHs because of the risk of retinal artery occlusion. Systemic corticosteroids may be an option for larger, deforming, or life-threatening lesions, during the growth phase. Prednisone or prednisolone can be given at doses of 2 to 4 mg/kg/d for 2 to 3 months and then gradually tapered over several months. An older Cochrane review found greater benefit with prednisolone than methylprednisolone at 3 months and 1 year. This dosage must be maintained until the functional risks subside. Very large IHs, with fast growth and atypical behavior, may require higher doses (up to 8 mg/kg/d).

Simultaneous administration of systemic and intralesional corticosteroids has been suggested. Alternatively, pulse therapy has been proposed consisting of cycles of 20 to 30 days at a dosage of 2 to 4 mg/kg/d of oral prednisone. Approximately 35% of patients will develop irritability, delayed skeletal growth, hypertension, immunosuppression, cushingoid appearance, and adrenal suppression.

Third-line therapy for IHs includes use of interferon alpha-2a or -2b. Subcutaneous doses of 1 to 3 million U/m2 interferon alpha-2a for 6 to 12 months may be indicated for enlarging IHs nonresponsive to beta-blockers or glucocorticoid therapy or for life-threatening complications. Side effects include neurotoxicity, transient neutropenia, elevated liver enzymes, fever, and malaise.
In recalcitrant lesions, sirolimus may be considered.

Another third-line pharmacologic therapy includes cytotoxins (eg, vincristine or vinblastine). Vincristine is preferred to interferon in life-threatening cases nonresponsive to beta-blocker or corticosteroid treatment. Low-dose cyclophosphamide has been successfully used in association with interferon alpha-2a for capillary IHs of the orbit.
Second-line therapy for IHs includes laser therapy and surgery.

Laser therapy may be considered for IHs refractory to beta-blockers or in cases that require urgent therapy (eg, potential airway compromise). The 2016 AHRQ report found laser treatment to have insufficient to low evidence of efficacy, with moderate evidence of harm (eg, dyspigmentation). Pulsed dye laser (PDL) appears to have the best evidence among the different laser modalities, and together with epidermal cooling technique, may be a good option to treat residual lesions after completing beta-blocker therapy.
The flash-lamp, pumped PDL has shown some efficacy in superficial IHs and residual lesions. Side effects include atrophic scarring, ulceration, and pain.
Combining oral propranolol with PDL may reduce propranolol duration without increasing harms. Additionally, PDL may accelerate healing.

For deep IHs, the neodymium-yttrium-aluminum-garnet laser has been used with promising results. Surgery is indicated for abnormal scar or excess tissue following natural involution, ulcerated lesions bleeding excessively, or lesions that interfere with development and/or activities such as lesions of the eye, ear, or larynx.
Therapeutic embolization may be used as a third-line option in alarming IHs. More commonly, it can be used in combination with pharmacologic or surgical therapy.
IHs are often a cause of distress for parents and may have a negative psychological impact on school-aged children. Education is an important part of therapy.

Intermittent pneumatic and continuous compression may be used to treat IHs in proliferative and involutive phases. Compression may be an effective treatment, particularly for IHs located on the extremities.

Cryosurgery has been recommended for treatment of raised lesions. Cryosurgery using a device with a constant applicator tip temperature of −32°C appears to have good cosmetic results and minor side effects.

Sclerotherapy consists of a sclerosing substance (eg, ethanolamine oleate, ethyl alcohol, monoethanolamine oleate, polidocanol, sodium tetradecyl sulfate) injected directly through the skin into a lesion. Sclerotherapy with monoethanolamine oleate was reported to be effective in the treatment of IHs with late involution. Sclerotherapy with polidocanol has been used on monstrous or rapidly growing IHs localized to the face with good long-term results.
Electrocautery consists of lesion destruction with high risk of scarring. One approach to treat patients with lingual hemangiomas is electro-acupuncture, which appears to have excellent results.
Consider hospitalization if local or major complications occur or refer to a specialist in the presence of associated syndromes.

Rapidly and diffusely growing hemangiomas may ulcerate in up to 10% of patients, especially during the first 9 months of life. Ulceration occurs more often in segmental IHs of the head and neck, and in IHs of the perineum and lip (24%-35%). Ulceration may cause disfigurement and functional compromise (eg, airway, auditory, visual).

Local wound care is the mainstay of treatment for ulcerative IHs. Compresses used for debridement of the ulcers can be used along with emollients or topical antibiotics (eg, mupirocin). As second-line therapy, becaplermin gel 0.01% has been reported to be effective for ulcerated perineal IHs.
Barrier dressings (eg, zinc oxide paste), occlusive dressings (eg, hydrocolloid), or topical antibiotics may be useful in areas prone to trauma or superinfection, such as the anogenital region.
Almost all hemangiomas will complete the involutional process by 12 years of age, but some may resolve incompletely. C

Although the majority of IHs are associated with a benign course, some cause complications (severe in about 10-15% of cases), including bleeding or ulceration and interference with breathing, vision, eating, or hearing. Large size, facial location, and/or segmental morphology are associated with a poorer outcome and may rarely result in increased morbidity or mortality. C

Regular follow-up visits are recommended to monitor the course of the lesions since their growth pattern may be unpredictable during the proliferative phase. Follow-up should be particularly close during the proliferative phase to determine early which IHs may require treatment. C

IHs exhibit a characteristic evolution. The earliest sign of an IH is blanching of the involved skin, which may be followed by fine telangiectasias and then by a red or crimson macule. Rarely, a shallow ulceration may be the first sign of an incipient IH.

The proliferative or growth phase occurs during the first year, with most of the growth occurring during the first 6 months of life. IHs become elevated and may be dome-shaped, lobulated, plaque-like, tumor-like, or any combination of these morphologies.

The involution may be rapid or prolonged. Fifty percent of IHs complete their involution by age 5 years and 70% by age 7 years; the remainder may take an additional 3 to 5 years to complete the process. During involution, IHs shrink centrifugally from the center of the lesion. This is less notable with deeper lesions. The superficial lesions become less red, taking on a duskier maroon to purple color, and finally regaining normal flesh tones.

IHs become softer and more compressible with decreased tenderness, and they exhibit less expansion during increased intravascular pressure (eg, crying). Approximately 50% to 60% of IHs resolve incompletely, leaving residual changes.
IHs lacking rapid progression and large extension, especially when found on the trunk and limbs, usually do not cause complications.

IHs can be part of serious, sometimes life-threatening, syndromes, such as PHACES syndrome (posterior fossa abnormalities, hemangiomas, arterial anomalies, cardiac anomalies, eye abnormalities, and sternal or abdominal clefting), SACRAL syndrome (lumbosacral hemangiomas, underlying spinal dysraphism or anorectal and urogenital anomalies), PELVIS syndrome (large perineal hemangioma, external genitalia malformations, lipomyelomeningocele, vesicorenal abnormalities, imperforate anus, and skin tag), and disseminated neonatal hemangiomatosis (multiple cutaneous IHs, visceral hemangiomatosis, most often hepatic and complicated by cardiac insufficiency or thyroid disease).

tr.td: Capillary (telangiectases and port-wine stains), venous, lymphatic, arteriovenous, and syndromic

Rare; 0.3%-0.5% of the population. Present at birth and grow commensurately with child growth; most become apparent growths throughout life; normal endothelial cell cycle; expansion with hormonal changes (eg, puberty, pregnancy), infection, trauma, or surgical intervention; related to Sturge-Weber and Klippel-Treneaunay syndromes

Rare, low-grade angiosarcoma primarily affecting the skin of children; histologic pattern of anastomosing vascular channels with intravascular papillary outpouchings sometimes projecting in a glomerulus-like pattern, into a lumen lined by atypical columnar endothelial cells
Rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH) and noninvoluting congenital hemangioma (NICH)
Fully grown in utero and do not proliferate postnatally like hemangiomas. RICH undergo spontaneous involution during the first year, while NICH persist lifelong

Rare; isolated tumors with presence of lymphatic endothelial cells in their proliferation; rapid and invasive growth; sometimes able to create platelet trapping, thrombocytopenia, and the life-threatening Kasabach-Merritt syndrome
